title: Confirm you have a Canadian-born or naturalized ancestor
description: Bill C-3 (effective 2025-12-15) removed the first-generation limit. If any direct ancestor was born in Canada or naturalized as a Canadian citizen, you may already be Canadian — no application required to BE a citizen, only to PROVE it.

title: Identify the Canadian-born or naturalized ancestor in your tree
description: Most often a parent, grandparent, or great-grandparent who was born in any modern Canadian province or territory, or who naturalized as a Canadian citizen. Pre-1947 'British subject' status in Canada also counts under the historical framework.

title: Map the documentary chain from you to the Canadian ancestor
description: Each generation needs: birth certificate, and where surnames change, marriage certificate. Note any gaps — those are your acquisition targets.

title: Check if Substantial Connection test applies
description: If you were born ON OR AFTER 2025-12-15 to a Canadian parent who is themselves a citizen by descent (born outside Canada), that parent must have spent ≥1,095 cumulative days physically in Canada before your birth. If you were born BEFORE 2025-12-15, the test does not apply — you are Canadian retroactively.

title: Request your own birth certificate (long-form)
description: Long-form (showing parents' names) is required, not the short-form / wallet-size version.

title: Request birth certificates for each ancestor in the chain
description: Order from each issuing jurisdiction — US state vital records office for US ancestors, provincial vital statistics for Canadian ancestors. Allow 4–12 weeks per certificate.

title: Search Library and Archives Canada for ancestor records
description: Census, military, and pre-1947 immigration/naturalization records. Free public access.

title: If your ancestor was Quebec-born, search BAnQ
description: Bibliothèque et Archives nationales du Québec — civil registry, parish records, Drouin Collection partner. Free digital access for most pre-1900 records.

title: Order marriage certificates for each generation where surnames change
If you need the Substantial Connection test, gather travel/residency proof
description: Passport stamps, immigration records, school records, employment records, tax records — anything that shows physical presence in Canada totaling ≥1,095 days for the relevant Canadian parent.

title: Complete IRCC Application for Proof of Canadian Citizenship
description: Form CIT 0001 (verify current form name on IRCC site at time of application). Submit online or by mail with all supporting documents.

links.label: IRCC: Apply for proof of citizenship

title: Pay the IRCC application fee
description: Confirm the current fee on the IRCC site at time of application — fees change. Currently CAD $75 for adults at last verification.

title: Wait for IRCC processing
description: Currently 6–12 months historically. Bill C-3 has created a substantial backlog so 2026 timelines may extend longer. Check the IRCC processing-times page periodically.

title: Receive your Canadian Citizenship Certificate
description: This is your official proof of Canadian citizenship. Keep it in a safe place — it's the foundation for your passport application.

title: Apply for a Canadian passport using your citizenship certificate
description: Submit Form PPTC 040 (adult simplified passport application). Your citizenship certificate serves as the primary proof.

title: Apply for a Social Insurance Number (SIN) if planning to work in Canada
description: Required to work or receive government benefits in Canada.

title: Understand your tax obligations as a dual US/Canadian citizen
description: The US taxes citizens on worldwide income regardless of residence. Canada taxes residents. The US-Canada tax treaty handles most overlap. Consider a CPA familiar with cross-border tax.

title: If you have children born abroad, document your physical presence in Canada
description: If they are born after 2025-12-15 and you want them to inherit Canadian citizenship by descent, you'll need ≥1,095 days physical presence in Canada before their birth — start the paper trail now.
